ground_truth.title: I Ran My Own Newsletter Through My AI Analysis Tool. Here's What I Found (And Why It Hurt)
ground_truth.author: Finn Tropy
ground_truth.main_content:
I build tools for Substack creators.

Specifically, I built StackContacts - a tool that pulls all your Substack data onto your own computer and uses AI to find patterns you can’t see in Substack’s dashboard.

For months, I’ve been telling other creators: “You need to understand your data. Growth isn’t random. Your audience is sending you signals.”

But here’s the embarrassing truth: I hadn’t run my own newsletter through the complete analysis.

Sure, I’d checked my subscriber count. Glanced at my stats. Told myself things were “pretty good.”

Then, last week, I decided actually to eat my own dog food.

I ran finntropy.substack.com through the same AI analysis I’ve been building for other creators.

What I found made me want to delete my LinkedIn profile and become a shepherd in New Zealand.

But it also showed me exactly why most Substack creators feel like they’re shouting into the void.

The Good News (That Made Me Feel Smart)

Let me start with the wins, because I need the dopamine (and more coffee):

86.8% of my subscribers are highly engaged.

Not “opened an email once” engaged. I’m talking 10+ interactions - opens, clicks, comments, the works.

The industry average? Somewhere between 20% and 30% if you’re doing well.

My average subscriber has engaged with 19.3 different posts. They’re clicking links (7.4 clicks per subscriber). They’re active across an average of 22 days.

My top-performing posts? They’re crushing it:

“How To Schedule Notes on Substack” - 3,806 views, 188 reactions, 91 comments

“ How Often Should You Publish Notes... ” - 2,919 views, 237 reactions, 95 comments

“ How I Turned My Substack Posts into Dividend-Paying Assets ” - 1,545 views, 105 reactions

For a newsletter with 1,193 subscribers and an annual sales revenue over $20k, these are legitimately strong numbers.

I felt pretty good about myself.
Look at me, crushing it with my engaged audience!

And then the AI showed me the ugly truth.

The Ugly Truth (That Made Me Want to Quit)

Here’s the data point that punched me in the throat:

100% of my new subscribers (who joined in the last 7 days) have never engaged with anything.

Not a single open. Not one click. Zero.

Twelve people signed up for my newsletter in the past week, excited enough to give me their email address, and I’ve done absolutely nothing to welcome them.

No welcome sequence. No “start here” post. No personal message.

I literally ghosted 100% of my new subscribers.

And it gets worse.

268 of my long-term subscribers haven’t engaged in 30+ days.

That’s 27% of my loyal readers slowly going dormant while I publish posts about “engagement strategies” and “audience building.”

The irony is so thick you could cut it with a knife.

But here’s where it gets truly painful:

I haven’t published a post in 22 days. Only three posts in the last 30 days.

The AI analysis showed my publishing frequency dropped from 11 posts in December 2024 to just 2-4 posts per month recently.

My newsletter about Substack growth strategies... has stopped growing because I stopped showing up consistently.

I am literally the person I write about helping.

The Pattern I Couldn’t See (Until AI Found It)

Here’s why this matters for you:

When I looked at my Substack dashboard, I saw:

“Engagement is strong” ✅

“Subscribers keep joining” ✅

“Popular posts are performing well” ✅

What I couldn’t see without AI analysis:

My New Subscriber Onboarding Is Broken

The AI compared engagement rates across subscriber cohorts:

New subscribers (0-7 days): 0% engaged

Recent subscribers (8-30 days): 94% engaged

Established subscribers (31-90 days): 100% engaged (none never-engaged)

The pattern was evident: If subscribers stick around past the first week, they become superfans. But I’m losing people in the first 7 days because I’m not giving them a reason to care.

My Publishing Frequency Directly Impacts Growth

The AI mapped posts published vs. new subscribers by month:

More posts ≠ more subscribers.

But consistent publishing = predictable growth.

My best month (July 2025) had only 3 posts but 54.33 subscribers per post.
My worst efficiency (December 2024) had 11 posts but only 7.45 subscribers per post.

The difference? Quality + timing + consistency.

I Know Exactly Which Content Types Work

The AI categorized all 75 of my posts and calculated performance by content type:

I have 36 posts in the “Other” category - basically filler content I published when I didn’t know what to write.

Those 36 posts got the lowest average views (457.8) and reactions (13.9).

Meanwhile, my 5 Strategy/Advice posts averaged 1,277.8 views and 96.4 reactions.

I’ve been publishing the wrong content 48% of the time.

And I had no idea until the AI showed me the pattern.

The Moment Everything Changed

I’ve built analysis tools professionally for years. I understand data. I know how to read spreadsheets.

But seeing my own publication laid out like this - with every pattern exposed, every failure highlighted, every missed opportunity quantified - hit different.

Because here’s what I realized:

Every Substack creator is flying blind.
Not because we’re stupid. Not because we don’t care.

But because the Substack dashboard shows you what happened, not why it happened or what to do about it.

You know you have 847 subscribers. Great.

How many are actually engaged? Which cohorts are at risk? What content types are working? When should you publish? Who are your superfans you should be building relationships with?

The dashboard can’t tell you.

So we make decisions based on vibes:

“Engagement feels low” (but is it actually low or just normal?)

“Growth feels random” (but is there a pattern you’re missing?)

“I don’t understand my audience” (but what if the data already shows you who they are?)

It’s like trying to drive across the country with a map that only shows which state you’re in. Technically useful. Practically useless.

What I Did Next (And What You Can Do Too)

I’m not going to pretend this article is purely altruistic.

I built StackContacts because I got tired of seeing talented creators give up because they couldn’t figure out what was working.

But after running my own analysis, here’s what I’m doing differently:

This Week:

✅ Creating a welcome sequence for new subscribers (no more 100% non-engagement)

✅ Sending a “I Miss You” email to those 268 dormant subscribers

✅ Publishing this post (getting back to consistency)

✅ Reaching out personally to my top 20 superfans (they’ve earned it)

This Month:

Publishing 1-2 posts per week minimum (no more excuses)

Doubling down on Strategy/Advice content (1,277.8 avg views vs 457.8 for “Other”)

Reducing filler “Other” content by 50%

Tracking which posts drive subscribers (using data, not vibes)

This Quarter:

Running this analysis monthly to track progress

Building relationships with the subscribers who are already engaged

Creating a content series based on my top-performing posts

Actually using my own tool consistently ( shocking concept, I know )

The Uncomfortable Question

If you’re still reading, you probably recognize yourself in this story.

You’ve got subscribers. You publish (sometimes). Engagement feels... fine?

But deep down, you know you’re flying blind. You’re making decisions based on what feels right instead of what the data shows.

And the Substack dashboard isn’t helping because it’s not designed to show you patterns - just metrics.

Here’s my uncomfortable question for you:

What if you’re making the same mistakes I was making?

What if you’re:

Ignoring your new subscribers without realizing it

Publishing the wrong content types 48% of the time

Watching engaged subscribers go dormant while you focus on vanity metrics

Missing obvious patterns in your growth because you don’t have the tools to see them

I built StackContacts to solve this exact problem.

Not because I’m a data genius (clearly, since I ghosted 100% of my new subscribers).

But because I got tired of watching creators - including myself - make preventable mistakes.

How This Actually Works (The Technical Bits)

Here’s what happens when you use StackContacts:

1. You Download Your Data

StackContacts pulls all your Substack data onto your own computer.
Subscribers, followers, events, posts, notes, engagement, everything.

Why your own computer? Because:

Your data stays private (no third-party storage)

You can analyze it offline anytime

No subscription fees for “data storage.”

You actually own your audience insights

2. AI Analyzes the Patterns

The tool runs your data through AI analysis to find:

Engagement patterns by subscriber cohort

Content performance by type

Growth correlations (publishing frequency, timing, topics)

At-risk subscribers who are going dormant

Your superfans who could become advocates

Specific, actionable recommendations

3. You Get Actual Insights

Not generic advice like “ post more consistently. ”

Specific insights like:

“Your Strategy/Advice posts get 2.8x more views than your Other content”

“100% of subscribers who make it past day 7 become highly engaged”

“268 subscribers haven’t engaged in 30+ days - here’s how to re-engage them”

“July 2025 had 54.33 subscribers per post vs December 2024’s 7.45 - here’s why”

The Real Reason This Matters

I spent the last 18 months building tools to help other creators grow.

Then I discovered I was failing at the basics.
Not because I didn’t care. Not because I’m lazy.

But because you can’t optimize what you can’t measure, and you can’t measure what you can’t see.

The Substack dashboard shows you the what.
AI analysis shows you the why and the what to do about it.

That’s the difference between “my growth feels random” and “I know exactly which content types drive subscribers and when to publish them.”

Between “I think engagement is okay?” and “86.8% of my subscribers are highly engaged, but 100% of new subscribers aren’t engaging because I don’t have a welcome sequence.”

Between guessing and knowing.

Try This Yourself

I’m not going to do a hard sell here.

If you’re skeptical about AI analysis tools, you should be. Most of them are garbage that spit out generic advice you could get from a blog post.

But here’s what I’ll offer:

Run your own analysis with the tool you can get from StackContacts.com
See what patterns you’re missing. Find out which content actually works.
Discover which subscribers are at risk.

If it’s useless, you’ll know in 10 minutes.

If it’s useful, you’ll have the exact same uncomfortable awakening I had:

“Oh no. I’ve been doing this wrong the whole time.”

And then you can actually fix it.

Because the only thing worse than discovering you’re failing 100% of your new subscribers...

...is never discovering it at all.

The Bottom Line

I built StackContacts to help creators grow.

Then I discovered I needed it more than anyone.

My newsletter has:

1,193 subscribers

86.8% highly engaged audience

Strong content performance

Proven content types that work

And I was still making critical mistakes I couldn’t see.

If I’m flying blind with tools and data experience, what chance do you have with just the Substack dashboard?

The answer isn’t to give up.

The answer is actually to look at the data.

Find the patterns.

Fix the problems.

Focus on what works.

And maybe - just maybe - stop ghosting 100% of your new subscribers.

Want to run your own analysis?

Download your Substack data and analyze it with AI using the StackContacts tool.

See what you’re missing. Fix what’s broken. Grow what’s working.

Your uncomfortable awakening is waiting.

— Finn

P.S. - After publishing this post, I’m sending welcome emails to those 12 new subscribers I ghosted. If you’re one of them and you’re reading this: I’m sorry. I was too busy building tools to help creators engage with their audiences, actually, to engage with my own. The irony is not lost on me.

P.P.S. - If you found this useful, reply and let me know what patterns you’re blind to in your own newsletter. I’m genuinely curious what other creators are missing that AI could help uncover.
